## Iteration 276 — the gate, priced at 137 cases

### The zero vector scores the published run

The count every screen in this repository reports is `Top@1`, and on a dump `Top@1` has two readings. The engine sorts
by score, stably, so a candidate **level** with the answer keeps its earlier position — and the dump's position is the
recorded order. So:

| Vector              |    strict | optimistic |
| ------------------- | --------: | ---------: |
| the shipped weights | **1 031** |      1 031 |
| the zero vector     |     **0** |  **1 073** |

**The empty vector answers the published run, all of it, by tie.** That is a spurious global optimum of the count
function, and it has been inside every ascent and every linear program this register has run since 272: iteration
275's constrained probe returned `w = 0` reporting "count 1 073" as an _improvement_ over the 1 031 baseline. Ties are
otherwise absent — one case in 1 422 carries one anywhere in its ranking under the shipped weights — so the two
readings agree wherever the weights are real, and the module now reports both (`readAt` strict, `optimistic`) and
credits only the strict one.

### The solver returned an unfinished tableau as an optimum

`maximise` carried a silent pivot budget. A 592-row program came back with `‖w‖₁ = 10.9` against a box that said `1`
and an objective of `0`, and that number was read as **"the gate cannot be cleared"**. It now throws
(`the pivot budget was exhausted`), the budget is a parameter, and the contract is asserted in the test file. This is
the second instrument defect this register has recorded in two iterations, and both were found by _disbelieving a
number_, not by reading the code.

### The gate's price

| Reading                                            |     Cases |        Share |
| -------------------------------------------------- | --------: | -----------: |
| The unconstrained fit (275)                        |      +154 |    +10.83 pp |
| The best gate-clean fit (3 seeds: +16 / +17 / +19) | **+17.3** | **+1.22 pp** |
| **What "no family may lose a case" costs**         |  **−137** | **−9.61 pp** |

The gate removes 89 % of the reachable gain. A gate-clean vector does exist — nine families gain, nine are unchanged,
none loses, and the fit is the first admissible weight change since 272 — but it is worth 1.2 pp, not 10.8. Held out,
the gain transfers (+7 to +22 on the unseen half in four fits of four) and the GATE does not (3 to 9 protected cases
lost on that half): the gate is a property of the corpus that states it, and a parameter fit cannot transfer it.

### Axes this closes

| Axis                                                 | Verdict                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| "A penalty on the gate will find the trade"          | **closed** — gate weights 1…256 buy +52…+145 at 21…116 lost gate cases; the exchange rate is the weight's, not the corpus's                                                 |
| "The count is a linear program over the artifact"    | **closed** — the count is Max FLS (Amaldi & Kann, TCS 147, 1995), NP-hard for homogeneous bipolar systems; with a mandatory subsystem no constant-factor guarantee survives |
| "One vector clears the gate AND gains double digits" | **closed** — 137 of the 154 cases the gate refuses are exactly what it will not allow                                                                                       |

### What this changes

The next subject is **per-case selection**, and its target is now quantitative rather than aspirational: one vector
inside the gate is worth `+17`, one vector outside it `+154`, and a per-case choice `+349`. The gate is a fence
around the middle of those three numbers, and the two outer ones are only reachable by a decision made per case.

---

## Iteration 277 — the recorded coefficient is a decision, and the baseline was never deployed

### The 42 cases

Every screen in this repository read a dump's coefficients out with "first appearance wins" and called the result the
shipped configuration. For `failedEdge` the first appearance is a **refusal**: the engine ranks once with the term
weighted out, asks a gate about its own rank-1, and returns the baseline when the gate says no — writing `0` into that
case's row. So the coefficient is `configured × admitted(case)`, the configured weight is `max` over what a dump
records, and the vector at `Δw = 0` (1 031) is the term **forced off everywhere**: a configuration nobody deployed.

| Reading                                          |     Cases |       Share |
| ------------------------------------------------ | --------: | ----------: |
| the configuration as one vector, term forced off |     1 031 |     72.50 % |
| **the run, rebuilt from its own coefficients**   | **1 073** | **75.46 %** |
| the configuration as one vector, term forced on  |     1 096 |     77.07 % |
| the per-case oracle over the two arms            |     1 186 |     83.40 % |

1 073 is 75.46 % of 1 422: the published RCABench cell. The artifact reproduces the run; the screens did not.

### The gate's ledger, for free

|          | cases |          fixed |        broken | neutral |
| -------- | ----: | -------------: | ------------: | ------: |
| admitted |   108 |             44 |             2 |      62 |
| refused  | 1 114 | 111 would have | 88 would have |     915 |

Admission is precise (44:2). Refusal is the cost centre: it gives up 111 to avoid 88, and the 111 are concentrated
where the term is strongest — 58 of them in `HTTPResponseReplaceCode` alone, a family the gate refuses wholesale
because a status-code fault fails calls instead of slowing them, so the rise bar that guards the term never sees it.

### Axes this closes

| Axis                                                              | Verdict                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| "The `failedEdge` zero is a configuration"                        | **closed** — it is the gate's refusal; `w = max S`, and `                                                                                                                   | S   | > 1` proves a name is a decision |
| "1 073 was the published run won by tie"                          | **corrected** — it is the run's own top-1, which a level vector reproduces by keeping the dump's order                                                                      |
| "A vector at `Δw = 0` reads the run"                              | **closed** — it cannot, while a conditional name is in the fusion; 1 031 and 1 096 are both real vectors and neither is the run                                             |
| "The term's per-case decision is unmeasurable without a dispatch" | **closed** — the dump carries both arms, so the ablation is arithmetic: 1 186 oracle, `+23` for deleting the gate, `−23` for the gate-clean fit of 276 read against the run |

### What this changes

Iteration 276's `+19` is `−23` against the run, and the vector it fitted is not an improvement — the gate-clean search
is searching inside a fence whose reference point was wrong. The next subject is the **gate's predicate**: the name
half admits 765 cases and the rise bar cuts them to 108, on a corpus where the term's own oracle is +113 over the run.
The question is no longer whether a per-case switch is worth building; it is which observable separates the 111 from
the 88.

## Iteration 278 — the 111 and the 88 are separated by the baseline's own lead, and the condition is what binds

277 ended with a question: the gate admits 108 cases (44 fixed, 2 broken) and refuses 1 114 (111 fixable, 88 would
have broken), so _which observable separates the 111 from the 88?_ Not the fault type, not the metric name, not the
rise, and **not the failed-call channel**: its score is max-normalised, so its maximum is 1.000 on every case in the
corpus and its top slope carries no information at all (the maximum sits at 1.000 at every decile of every outcome).
It is the **lead** — the baseline ranking's first candidate minus its second, in units of what the term could ever
move.

### The frontier

`benchmarks/src/gate-rejector.ts` reads a dump as (lead, reach, run coefficient) and prices every bound; the run's
own admissions stay a floor, so a gate change is measured on the population it ships to.

| reach |     cases |   delta | helps | hurts | loss | families that lose a case |
| ----: | --------: | ------: | ----: | ----: | ---: | ------------------------- |
|  0.02 |     1 123 |     +50 |    58 |     8 |    4 | 3 families, worst −2      |
|  0.10 | **1 145** | **+72** |    95 |    23 |   15 | 6 families, worst −7      |
|  0.20 | **1 145** | **+72** |   104 |    32 |   19 | 7 families, worst −8      |
|  0.30 | **1 145** | **+72** |   110 |    38 |   23 | 8 families, worst −8      |
|  0.35 | **1 145** | **+72** |   111 |    39 |   24 | 8 families, worst −9      |
|  1.00 |     1 096 |     +23 |   111 |    88 |   70 | 11 families, worst −18    |

Three readings:

- **the total is flat over a factor of three in the bound** (0.10 to 0.35 all answer 1 145), so the corpus offers an
  interval rather than a point;
- **no bound satisfies the standing condition** — the cheapest violation is 4 loss units at 0.02 — so the condition,
  not the statistic, is now what binds;
- **reach 1.00 reproduces 277's always-on arm exactly** (1 096, +23), which is the check on the reader: the frontier
  degenerates to the constant arm when the bound stops excluding anything, because the 180 cases with a reach in
  `[1, 2]` are all neutral.

### Out of fold

| rate |  held out |   run |   delta | loss | bounds chosen                     |
| ---: | --------: | ----: | ------: | ---: | --------------------------------- |
|    1 | **1 142** | 1 073 | **+69** |   26 | 0.310, 0.310, 0.222, 0.292, 0.310 |
|    3 |     1 131 | 1 073 |     +58 |   17 | 0.025, 0.101, 0.190, 0.079, 0.086 |

The bound reproduces itself on every fold at rate 1 and the out-of-fold total is **three cases below the in-sample
one**. The Chow bound is derived rather than scanned: the isotonic fit of `p(fixes | reach)` crosses `1/2` between the
seventh and eighth brackets, i.e. at a lead of about one unit — a third of the span.

### Axes this closes

| Axis                                                             | Verdict                                                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| "The 111 are a class, not a margin"                              | **closed** — `p(fix)` is 0.75–0.90 below one span and 0.09 then 0.00 above it, monotone in a quantity computed before the gate decides                  |
| "The gate's predicate is the lever"                              | **half closed** — the predicate is worth +72, and the condition that refused the earlier arms refuses this one by 15 to 24 units                        |
| "The failed-call channel's own score can be read on this corpus" | **closed** — max-normalised to 1.000 everywhere; a saturated quantity cannot rank                                                                       |
| "A lead above one span cannot be flipped"                        | **corrected before it was claimed** — 11 cases above one span still flip (the promoted candidate need not be the runner-up), and the term is right once |

### What ships

`failedEdgeGateMode: 'margin'` is now a member of the closed vocabulary, with `share` a fraction of the term's own
span (`DEFAULT_FAILED_EDGE_MARGIN_SHARE = 0.3`). The default stays `absolute`, so every published cell is unchanged;
the mode is an arm a run selects, and what the record holds is the frontier rather than the constant.

The frontier's own record is `docs/gate-rejector.md`: the statistic's arithmetic, Chow's rule and the isotonic fit,
the two tables above as the module prints them, and the four axes the readback settles. This section is the verdict;
that document is the instrument.

## Iteration 279 — the condition has a price, and the cheapest rung is two

278 ended with the condition binding: no bound of the reach statistic meets "no regressed fault type", and the
cheapest violation costs 4 loss units. That is a statement about a veto, and a veto is not a decision — the next
measurement is the condition as a **budget**: no family may lose more than `k` cases. `budgetScanOf` reads the same
frontier at every `k`, `cheapestOf` prices the frontier itself, and `pnpm tsx benchmarks/src/run-gate-rejector.ts
--terms <dump>` prints both. `docs/gate-rejector.md` §7 is the instrument's record.

### The ladder

The run is 1 073. Every rung keeps the run's own admissions as a floor, so the deltas are against the configuration a
gate change would actually ship to.

|   `k` | reach |     cases |   delta | loss | cases bought per case lost | families that pay                                                |
| ----: | ----: | --------: | ------: | ---: | -------------------------: | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
|     0 |     — |         — |       — |    — |                          — | the standing condition: no bound meets it                        |
|     1 |     — |         — |       — |    — |                          — | nothing on the grid is that cheap                                |
| **2** |  0.02 | **1 123** | **+50** |    4 |                   **12.5** | `HTTPRequestDelay` −2, `HTTPRequestReplacePath` −1, `PodKill` −1 |
|   4–6 |  0.05 |     1 131 |     +58 |    8 |                        7.3 | five families, worst −4                                          |
|  7–10 |  0.10 | **1 145** | **+72** |   15 |                        4.8 | six families, worst −7                                           |

### Three readings

- **The cheapest rung is 2, not 1.** Every point of the frontier loses at least two cases in one family: the bound
  whose deepest family loss is smallest is 0.02, and there `HTTPRequestDelay` loses 2. A ladder printed only at 0 and 1
  would have read as "no trade exists", which is why the ladder prints a cheapest-rung line as well as its rungs.
- **The peak costs 7, not the 9 guessed in 278.** The guess was read off the SUMMED loss at 0.35 (24 units), and a sum
  cannot answer a per-family question: the total is best at 0.10, where the deepest family loses 7. The sum overstates
  the price by two rungs, and a reader who priced the sum would have overpaid for the same 1 145.
- **The trade diminishes steeply.** 12.5 cases bought per case sacrificed at the cheapest rung, 4.8 at the peak. The
  cheapest compliant number is therefore also the most efficient one, and the peak costs 2.6× as much per case — so
  "answer as many cases as possible" and "buy cases efficiently" are different rungs of the same frontier.

### Axes this closes

| Axis                                                  | Verdict                                                                                                                                                            |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| "The condition can be bought for one case per family" | **closed** — no point of the grid loses fewer than 2 in one family; the floor is `HTTPRequestDelay` at 0.02                                                        |
| "`k = 9` reproduces the peak"                         | **corrected before it was claimed** — the peak's rung is 7, because the peak sits at 0.10 and the deepest family there loses 7; the 9 came from 0.35's summed loss |
| "The summed loss prices the condition"                | **closed** — a per-family condition cannot be priced by a sum: 0.10 and 0.35 differ by 9 loss units and answer the same total                                      |
| "The cheapest rung is the peak's rung"                | **closed** — 2 versus 7; efficiency and total are different orderings of the same frontier                                                                         |

### What ships

`budgetScanOf`, `cheapestOf`, `DEFAULT_LOSS_BUDGETS` and `formatBudgets` are in `benchmarks/src/gate-rejector.ts`,
with the ladder printed by the command that prints the frontier. No engine default moves: the shipped mode is still
`absolute`, and the ladder is a reading rather than a selection. The condition stays the register's to relax, and it
now has a price list instead of a veto.

### The four checks

**Competitors.** RCAtlas-Core (Bi, Zhang, Li, Wang and Ma, Peking University and BUPT, arXiv 26 October 2026) pools
eight public RCA datasets into 90 validated cases over 23 scenarios and three label levels (service 59, pod 20,
node 11), with injection-tool traces removed. Its headline result reorganises the field: **simple harnesses beat
hand-crafted agents on every model tested** — Codex 77.2 % PR@1, SQL-agent 72.8 %, one-shot 65.3 % on three mid-tier
models, against the best published agent at 53.3 %, the best non-LLM method at 38.9 % and random at 5.5 %; the best
single run reaches 88.9 % at about 26¢ per case. Two of their ablations bear directly on this register: a stronger
model buys **reliability** (solved-only-sometimes falls 32–36 % → 7–8 %) while a multi-turn harness buys **ceiling**,
and raising reasoning effort adds 2–4 points at 1.5–4× the wall time. The measurement consequence for us is blunt:
**80.52 % on RCABench is not comparable with PR@1 on RCAtlas-Core**, and no SOTA claim survives without a run on that
set. Their prescribed-call statistic (0.10–1.00 for the hand-crafted agents, 0.00 for the free harnesses) is also the
right instrument for our own agentic arm: it prices exactly the thing III.2 built.

**Evaluation sets.** RCAtlas-Core (`core90_cases.csv`) and LEMMA-RCA (CIKM '26, public via `lemmarca.info`, Zenodo
DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20516735) are both still outside our corpus. Neither is a gap in our numbers; both are a gap in
what our numbers can be compared to.

**Mathematics.** The budget axis is measured and **not guaranteed**. Conformal risk control (Angelopoulos, Bates,
Fisch, Lei and Schuster, ICLR 2024) chooses `λ̂ = inf{λ : n/(n+1)·R̂_n(λ) + B/(n+1) ≤ α}` and gives a finite-sample,
distribution-free bound on the expected loss; the multi-`λ` extension (arXiv 2406.18777) covers per-coordinate losses,
which is exactly a per-family budget; and learn-then-test (Angelopoulos et al., 2025) drops the monotonicity
requirement and, through fixed-sequence testing, exploits an ordered grid — which our bound ladder is. So the honest
statement about the ladder above is: it prices the condition **on this corpus**, and it carries no guarantee off it.
That is the next mathematical step, not a caveat to file.

**CI.** Green at `60139d0f` and at `81495a0b`, with Dependabot and code-scanning alerts at zero.

## Iteration 280 — the ladder is an estimate, and the certificate costs nine cases of budget

279 closed with a number and an admission: 1 123 cases for two lost in one family, and no guarantee off this corpus.
The budget has now been certified, and the certificate is larger. `benchmarks/src/risk-control.ts` reads the frontier
this register already records, prices every family's losses with the exact Clopper–Pearson upper end, splits the level
across families by a union bound, and selects the widest bound whose worst family still clears the budget.
`docs/risk-control.md` is the instrument's record; this section is the verdict.

### The certified ladder

n = 1 422, level 0.05, 25 families, so each family is held to 0.002. `tsx benchmarks/src/run-gate-rejector.ts --terms
<dump> --budget 11 --budget 14 --budget 22`:

| budget | bound |     cases |   delta | worst family       | lost |   upper | vs 279's estimate |
| -----: | ----: | --------: | ------: | ------------------ | ---: | ------: | ----------------- |
| **11** |  0.02 | **1 123** | **+50** | `HTTPRequestDelay` |    2 | 0.00729 | was k = 2         |
|     14 |  0.05 |     1 131 |     +58 | `HTTPRequestDelay` |    4 | 0.00971 | was k = 4–6       |
|     22 |  0.10 | **1 145** | **+72** | `HTTPRequestDelay` |    7 | 0.01301 | was k = 7–10      |

Nothing between k = 2 and k = 10 certifies anything, so the default ladder (0–10) prints eleven empty rungs and a
footer naming 11 as the smallest budget that does. At level 0.01 the same point moves to 13, so the count dominates
the level by an order of magnitude.

### Three readings

- **Certainty costs nine cases of budget at the cheapest rung.** 279 priced the condition at k = 2; the interval for
  two losses of 1 422 is 0.00729, and the first rung above it is 11. The +50 is unchanged — what changed is that it
  now survives a 95 % claim over 25 families, which the +50 at k = 2 did not.
- **The peak survives, and that is the real result.** +72 was the number most at risk of being a small-corpus artefact,
  and it certifies at 22. The finding stands; only its price was understated.
- **One family binds all three rungs.** `HTTPRequestDelay` is the worst family at 0.02, 0.05 and 0.10, so the budget
  is spent on one family's variance. A rung that bought cases without deepening that family would be cheaper than any
  rung in this table, and that is now the most concrete target the ladder has.

### Axes this closes

| Axis                                             | Verdict                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| "The point-estimate budget is the budget"        | **closed** — 2 against 11; the estimate is a lower bound on the price, never the price                                                                                                                  |
| "No regressed fault type is a guarantee"         | **closed** — zero losses of `n` rule out rates above `−ln δ/n`, so the veto is not certifiable at budget 0 at ANY corpus size (the rule of three: floor(0, 0.05) = 3)                                   |
| "More cases buy a cheaper budget"                | **closed** — `n·upper(lost, n)` converges (6.24 → 6.30 from 245 to a million cases), so a family losing 2 certifies at 7 whatever `n` is; more data buys a smaller share, not a smaller count           |
| "Multiplicity is a detail"                       | **closed** — the same losses at a per-family level need 7/10/14 and simultaneously 11/14/22; the 25-family claim costs 4/4/8 cases of budget                                                            |
| "A corpus with no families certifies everything" | **closed by construction** — an empty `every` certified every bound in the grid until a test asked for a corpus with no cases; `certifyOf` now requires a corpus AND a family before it makes any claim |

### What ships

`exactUpperOf`, `binomCdfUpTo`, `populationOf`, `risksAt`, `certifyOf`, `thresholdOf`, `floorOf`, `formatCertified`,
at 100 % on all four dimensions over 52 tests whose reference values come from `scipy.stats.beta.ppf` rather than from
this implementation, plus `--delta` on the rejector's command line. No engine default moves: the certified ladder is a
reading, and `absolute` is still the shipped mode.

The rejected axis is recorded rather than pursued: a max-statistic bootstrap over the corpus would exploit the
dependence between families instead of assuming none, and would certify 11 at something under 11. It is not
implemented, because a bootstrap buys tightness with an asymptotic argument where the union bound buys exactness with
none — and this register's whole complaint about 279 was that a number without a guarantee is not a claim.

## Iteration 280b — the correction was loose, and the certificate costs nothing

§280 was pushed with a union bound split across 25 families and a verdict of 11/14/22. Within the same iteration the
split was measured against the alternative, and the alternative wins: **Holm's step-down certifies the same three
numbers at 7, 10 and 14** — exactly the floors of `floorOf`, which is the proof that the 4/4/8 difference was slack
rather than price. `Correction` is now a parameter of `certifyOf` and `thresholdOf`, the command prints both rules, and
`docs/risk-control.md` records both.

### The two readings, side by side

| cases | delta |  Holm | union | floor (§4) | verdict                 |
| ----: | ----: | ----: | ----: | ---------: | ----------------------- |
| 1 123 |   +50 | **7** |    11 |          7 | Holm lands ON the floor |
| 1 131 |   +58 |    10 |    14 |         10 | Holm lands ON the floor |
| 1 145 |   +72 |    14 |    22 |         14 | Holm lands ON the floor |

### Why the union bound was the loose one

A union bound holds every family to `δ/F = 0.002` and pays for 25 claims whether or not any of them needs paying for.
The corpus's 24 clean families have tails of about `1e-3` against that threshold, so they consume almost none of the
level and the binding family is left with `δ/25` when it could be read at `δ`. A step-down procedure is entitled to
spend the evidence in order: it rejects the most extreme family first at `δ/F`, and the least extreme one — which can
only be reached after every other rejection — at `δ` itself. This is not a tightening of the claim; it is the same
claim, and its family-wise error rate is exactly `δ` under arbitrary dependence.

The cost of the mistake is worth naming because the loose rule is the one a careful implementer writes first: it is
valid, it is conservative, and it is wrong by a factor of nearly two in the currency this module spends. Nothing in
the code was broken; a theorem was left on the table.

### Axes this closes

| Axis                                                           | Verdict                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| "The certified budget is 11"                                   | **superseded** — 7; §280's table is what a union bound costs, and it was in the tree for one commit                                                                                                                            |
| "Multiplicity over 25 families costs 4/4/8 cases"              | **closed as slack** — Holm costs 0 against the floor, so the width of the claim is free here and the union bound was paying for evidence it already had                                                                        |
| "Holm and the union bound can disagree in the other direction" | **closed by test** — Holm dominates: `certifyOf` is asserted to certify every point the union bound does, over five budgets                                                                                                    |
| "An empty population certifies everything"                     | **closed twice** — the guard moved from the caller into `supports`, where it is the one place that decides a claim with no families cannot be made, and it is exercised by the empty-corpus test rather than being unreachable |

### What ships

`Correction = 'union' | 'holm'` on `certifyOf`, `thresholdOf` and `formatCertified`; the header states the rule, because
a budget without its rule cannot be compared with another budget. 58 tests, 100 % on all four dimensions. The engine's
defaults are untouched, as they have been for the whole of this thread: `absolute` is still the shipped gate mode.

## Iteration 281 — the certificate has to pay for the selection

The weight screen prints 28 rows and names none of them; the reader ships one. Every budget in §280 priced that row as
though it had been formulated in advance, and no row of a ranking table is. **A claim about the best of `M` candidates
has to pay for the `M` looks**, and paying with the level (`δ/M`) is Bonferroni's adjustment — the same correction
Benjamini & Yekutieli apply to intervals around selected parameters, exact rather than asymptotic.

The price is measured, on the 1 422-case dump, for the row the point estimate prefers (`stability 0.3 + log 1.2`, +13):

| reading                          | corpus | budget | rate      |
| -------------------------------- | -----: | -----: | --------- |
| single — named in advance        |  1 422 |  **8** | **0.56 %** |
| joint — best of 28 on this corpus |  1 422 | **13** | **0.91 %** |
| split, 2 folds                   |    711 |    7.5 | 1.05 %    |
| split, 5 folds                   |    284 |    7.0 | 2.46 %    |
| split, 10 folds                  |    142 |    7.0 | 4.92 %    |

The naive reading is 1.6× optimistic, which is the winner's curse in this repository's own currency. A 2-fold split
prices the same row at 1.05 %, so **28 looks cost about what half the corpus costs** — and the deeper splits show the
floor again: the budget stays at 7 whatever the fold size, so a split can only pay for itself in corpus, never in
count.

### The selection on the real corpus

`pnpm tsx benchmarks/src/run-term-weight-screen.ts --terms <dump>`, `δ = 0.05`, Holm, 28 looks, 29 readings:

| candidate                          | cases | delta | budget | worst family        | lost | price | verdict         |
| ---------------------------------- | ----: | ----: | -----: | ------------------- | ---: | ----: | --------------- |
| shipped                            | 1 073 |     0 |     10 | `ContainerKill`     |    0 |     — | unchanged       |
| stability 0.05                     | 1 074 |    +1 | **10** | `HTTPRequestDelay`  |    1 |     — | **improvement** |
| stability 0.1                      | 1 075 |    +2 |     11 | `HTTPRequestDelay`  |    2 | 2.000 | concession      |
| log 1.2                            | 1 073 |     0 |     14 | `HTTPRequestDelay`  |    4 |     — | **flat**        |
| stability 0.3 + log 1.2            | 1 086 |   +13 |     13 | `HTTPResponseDelay` |    3 | 4.333 | concession      |
| stability 0.3 + lat 0.4 + log 1.2  | 1 078 |    +5 |     16 | `HTTPRequestDelay`  |    5 | 0.833 | concession      |

29 readings resolve as **1 improvement, 12 concessions, 12 regressions, 1 flat, 3 unchanged**. The single improvement
is worth one case — and it is the one row the standing acceptance condition already rejects (it costs
`HTTPRequestDelay` a case), so the two instruments say different things about it and both are right: a family above the
floor did lose a case, and no family lost more than the shipped run's certified claim of ten.

### The two rules, priced

|              | shipped | `stability 0.05`       | `stability 0.3 + log 1.2` | best price | certified improvements |
| ------------ | ------: | ---------------------- | ------------------------: | ---------: | ---------------------- |
| **union**    |      10 | 13 — concession, 0.333 |                        20 |  **1.857** | none                   |
| **holm**     |      10 | **10 — improvement**   |                    **13** |  **4.333** | `stability 0.05`       |

Holm is worth more here than it was on the ladder: under the union bound **no row can be certified to improve on what
ships**, and the best price is less than half. At `δ = 0.01` both budgets rise by two (10 → 12, 13 → 15) and the price
stays **4.333**: a claim's cost in cases per unit conceded is a property of the corpus, its level is a property of the
reader's appetite for being wrong.

### Two defects the work found

- **`thresholdOf` returned the corpus's own size when nothing certified.** The bisection's upper end is a number
  whatever the claim at that end says, so a one-case corpus reported "cheapest certifiable: 1" — the vacuity the
  empty-family guard already refuses one level up, and a test had been written to call that ceiling honest. It now
  checks the ceiling and returns `null`; the test asserts the refusal beside the count that explains it
  (`floorOf(1, 0.05) = 5 > n = 1`) and the same count certifying on a corpus large enough to price it.
- **The screen's loss list is floor-filtered, and a certificate read off it would be narrower than the corpus.** A
  family of three losing three cases vanishes from `losses` because a family of four cannot sentence a move — but a
  claim is about every family. Rows now carry `ledger` (whole) beside `losses` (filtered) and the report carries
  `families`, so both readings come from one measurement rather than two.

### Axes this closes

| Axis                                                       | Verdict                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| "A screen row's budget is the certificate's budget"         | **closed** — the row was named after looking at 28 rows; pricing it as a hypothesis named in advance is 1.6× optimistic (0.56 % against 0.91 %)                                           |
| "Multiplicity over candidates is prohibitively expensive"   | **closed as measured** — 28 looks cost about half the corpus (0.91 % against 1.05 % at 2 folds), and the count floor means deeper splits can only lose                                   |
| "Splitting the corpus removes the need for the correction"  | **half-closed** — it removes the multiplicity and pays 2.8× the rate at 5 folds; the 2-fold split is the near-equivalent, not the free one                                                 |
| "The best row is the best buy"                              | **closed** — `stability 0.1` buys 2 cases per budget unit and `stability 0.3 + log 1.2` buys 4.333, but `stability 0.05` buys one for nothing, and `log 1.2` buys nothing for four          |
| "A row that ties on cases is a tie"                         | **closed** — `log 1.2` answers the shipped 1 073 at a budget of 14 instead of 10, which is a concession of four units for nothing                                                          |

### What ships

`docs/certified-selection.md` is the instrument's record; this section is the verdict.
`benchmarks/src/certified-selection.ts` (`selectCertified`, `formatSelection`) at 100 % on all four dimensions over 31
tests, `certifyLosses` / `risksOf` / `worstOf` / `lossesOf` exported from `risk-control.ts`, an `examined` parameter on
`certifyOf` / `thresholdOf` (one by default, so §280's tables stand as the marginal reading), `ledger` and `families` on
the screen, and `--delta` / `--correction` on the screen's command line so the level and the rule can be ablated without
editing the tree. The screen still selects nothing and the engine's defaults are untouched: `absolute` is the shipped
gate mode.

## Iteration 282 — the ceiling had no method under it, and the method now has an artifact

`scoreArm` has carried four arms since iteration 267: `engine`, `oracle`, `evidence` and `recorded`. Three of them
could be produced by the repository. The fourth — the one whose own docblock says *"replays claims somebody else
proposed, which is how a model's answers are scored without calling it again"* — had **no producer anywhere in the
tree**. So the elimination line could price a bound and a deterministic rule, and could not answer the question the
bound exists to ask, which is whether a model collects any of it. Fifteen iterations of instruments, and the arm
that costs money was the one with nothing behind it.

**This iteration is the producer and nothing else.** It ships five modules and a command; it moves no published
number, because no dispatch has run the paid arm. That state is recorded here rather than discovered later.

### What the model is allowed to say, and what it is not offered

| decision                                        | why                                                                                                              |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| the reply is JSON, one object, one array          | a prose answer and a wrong answer are the same object until scored — the reason `0d6ae609` retired the first layer |
| an **empty array is a legitimate answer**        | "the ranking is right" is an outcome; pooling it with "no answer" would make a silent model look confident        |
| `delta` is **not offerable**                     | it is the one statistic the table does not print, so quoting it means computing it, and a rounding error reads as fabrication |
| every number is printed as `String(v)`           | the verifier compares with `===`, so a faithful copy must round-trip exactly                                      |
| a malformed element refuses the **whole reply**  | a truncated answer's surviving claims are an accident of generation order, and admitting them makes accuracy a function of `max_tokens` |

### Three refusals on the way back, kept apart

`replayOf` refuses a recorded answer whose `digest` disagrees with the prompt this build produces (`stale`), whose
`protocol` is another version (`foreignProtocol`), or whose case is not in the population (`unknown`). One combined
count would let a single number stand for three different mistakes: a changed prompt, a changed parser, and a
claims file scored against the wrong corpus.

**A failed call is an abstention, not a dropped case.** A transport failure is recorded with its reason and the
digest of the question that was asked, so the case stays in the denominator and a resumed run does not pay for it
twice. The alternative — dropping the case — would let an outage improve the accuracy by shrinking the population.

### Three defects the work found, and one the census found in itself

- **A resumed run appended every reused line a second time.** `proposeClaims` called `onRecord` for records it had
  just *reused*, so the claim file grew by one line per resumed case and a run that asked nothing reported a file
  twice its size. The resume test failed on the line count; the fix is to count a reuse and not emit it.
- **`createChatClientFromEnv` returned two different shapes.** The key-present branch had no `reason` and the
  key-absent one did, which the compiler only reported when the study needed to print the reason from either. Both
  branch to `{ client, reason }` now, with `''` for "there was nothing to report".
- **`populationOf`'s comparator had an equality arm no corpus can reach.** `joinHeadroom` consumes a verdict as it
  pairs it and reports the second fingerprint of a duplicate as unpaired, so two cases cannot share a datapack. The
  third arm was deleted rather than covered — the same rule §267 applied to two guards in the fingerprint builder.
- **The comparator census could not READ the eliminator's channel order.** `signatureOf` derives a site's signature
  from the comparison a tie-break applies, and its operand is written on the sort's own two arguments — so a
  comparator written on `left`/`right` derives as the window's tail, which is not a signature and cannot be
  enrolled. The site was therefore invisible to an instrument that claims its population is derived. The fix is
  the one the census asks for and the code wanted anyway: decorate each channel once (`departureOf` ran up to three
  times per comparison before) and write every arm as `a.<field>` against `b.<field>`. `packages/ai/src` joins the
  census's roots in the same commit, because a comparator outside the population is a comparator nobody measures —
  and the first site in `packages/ai` is this one.

The census is the only one of the four that failed on the *first* push and was right to: it refused a tree in which
`benchmarks/src/agentic-eliminator-study.ts` sorted by datapack without stating its population. Enrollment, not
exemption, is the rule; the entry states why the two-arm form is safe (the headroom join makes datapacks unique).

### What the first reading will be judged on, stated before it exists

1. **ceiling gap** — `recorded` against `oracle` on the same population: how much of the verifiable headroom a cheap
   model collects. §267 measured that ceiling at **+16.63 pp** over 711 cases with 3 rounds covering 95 % of them.
2. **refusal rate** — `value-disagrees-with-fingerprint` against the claim count. This is the one number that
   separates "the model reasons badly" from "the model cannot copy a table", and they call for different fixes.
3. **the price** — the certified budget of the arm's delta at `δ`, computed by §280's function with the level split
   over **every family in the population**. A gain quoted without it is the reading §276 refused for the weight
   vector, one axis over.

### The first reading, dispatched before this section was written

Run `43548386087` on `7e17d26`, corpus `corpus-release-282`, model asked `deepseek-chat`, model **served
`deepseek-flash`** — recorded from the endpoint's own reply rather than from the request, which is the one place a
reader can tell a router from a model.

| arm        | top1      | moves | claims | silent | delta                |
| ---------- | --------: | ----: | -----: | -----: | -------------------- |
| `engine`   | **75.5 %** |     0 |      0 |      0 | control              |
| `oracle`   | 87.7 %    |   174 |    269 |  1 248 | **+174** (ceiling)   |
| `evidence` | 44.2 %    |   695 |    695 |    727 | **−444**             |
| `recorded` | 33.1 %    |   925 |  5 335 |    348 | **−602**, worst family −88 |

Proposal: 1 422 asked, 1 421 answered, **0 declined**, 1 unreadable (`the reply is not JSON`), 5 335 claims,
3 244 994 prompt + 354 585 completion tokens, 421 s, p50 1 798 ms per call.

**The three pre-registered criteria, read in order.**

1. **ceiling gap: −602 of +174.** The model does not collect a fraction of the ceiling; it destroys 602 cases the
   engine already had, and the ceiling itself is +174 above the engine. There is no gap to close — the arm is
   below the control by 8× the headroom that exists.
2. **refusal rate: 2 014 of 5 335 (37.8 %)**, and the decomposition is the whole finding:

   | refusal                              | count | share of claims |
   | ------------------------------------ | ----: | --------------: |
   | `unknown-channel`                    | 1 774 |          33.2 % |
   | `band-disagrees-with-fingerprint`    |   207 |           3.9 % |
   | `removed-candidate-is-inside-its-band` |    28 |           0.5 % |
   | `rate-disagrees-with-fingerprint`    |     4 |           0.1 % |
   | `value-disagrees-with-fingerprint`   |     1 |           0.0 % |

   **Arithmetic is not the problem — the contract is.** `value-disagrees` fires once in 5 335 claims, so copying a
   printed number is something this model does essentially perfectly. `unknown-channel` fires 1 774 times because
   `verifyClaim` requires the cited channel to exist on **both** the removed and the kept candidate, and the prompt
   states only the first half ("one channel that the candidate you eliminate left") while the table prints each
   candidate's channels independently. Measured on the same artifact: the five presented candidates share **2.2
   labels on average (median 2), and 56 of 1 422 cases share none**; of the 5 335 claims, 3 561 (66.7 %) cite a
   label present on both, 774 only on the removed candidate, 742 only on the kept one, and 258 on neither. All 240
   non-channel refusals fall inside the 3 561, so **acceptance among claims that clear the channel rule is 93.3 %**.
3. **price: not computed.** `certifiedBudgetOf` prints 105 for the arm and the number is meaningless on a delta of
   −602 — a budget is the corpus's permission for a gain, and there is no gain to permit. The row is printed so a
   reader sees the function agree rather than the study hide it.

**Two behavioural facts the artifact holds that no table prints.** 1 253 of 1 422 replies used the full four-claim
bound and exactly **one** was an empty array, so the model never once said "the ranking is right" — on a corpus
where the engine is right 75.5 % of the time. And the `evidence` arm at the same weight collapses to 44.2 %
(−444): mechanical elimination on departure is not a signal either, so a repaired channel contract is **necessary
and not sufficient**, and the next arm has to change what is asked, not only how it is spelled.

### Axes this closes

| Axis                                                          | Verdict                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| "The recorded arm can be scored"                               | **closed** — `run-agentic-eliminator.ts --propose` produces the claims, verifies them through the same `verifyClaim` every other arm uses, and scores all four |
| "A cached answer is only valid for the question that elicited it" | **closed** — the prompt digest and the protocol version are recorded per line, and a replay refuses a mismatch by name                                    |
| "An ablation of the model arm needs a second dispatch"          | **closed** — `--weight`, `--max-candidates` and `--skip-rule` are re-reads of the claims file; `--weight 0` is the control by construction                  |
| "A failed call may be dropped from the population"              | **closed** — it is recorded as an abstention with its reason, so an outage cannot improve the score                                                         |
| "The prompt may ask for a statistic the model must compute"      | **closed** — `delta` is excluded from the protocol; the two quotable statistics are the two the table prints                                                |
| "The paid arm can be measured without a key"                    | **closed as measured** — the study prints `MODEL ARM NOT MEASURED: <reason>` and exits non-zero; the workflow warns by name, so a green job cannot imply a row that was never produced |
| "Replaying a claim is a method"                                 | **closed as REFUTED on its first reading** — 33.1 % against a 75.5 % control, −602 cases, measured on 1 422 cases with 5 335 claims; the arm is an ablation that costs money and loses to doing nothing |
| "A prompt may name a comparison the table cannot express"       | **closed** — the verifier requires the cited channel on both candidates and the prompt asked for one on the removed one; 33.2 % of claims died there. The protocol must print which presented ranks share a label, or not ask for a shared one |

### What ships

`docs/agentic-eliminator.md` is the instrument's record; this section is the verdict.
`packages/ai/src/agent/eliminator.ts` (**100/100/100/100**, 26 tests), `benchmarks/src/agentic-claims.ts`
(**100/100/100/100**, 15 tests), `benchmarks/src/chat-completions.ts` (**100/100/100/100**, 15 tests, against a real
loopback socket), `benchmarks/src/agentic-proposer.ts` (**100/100/100**, 13 tests),
`benchmarks/src/agentic-eliminator-study.ts` (**100/100/100**, 16 tests, driving the whole study over real
artifacts), `certifiedBudgetOf` on the arm module, `byFamily` on `ArmOutcome` — the per-family view of the same
increment the `top1` column is printed from, so a table and a ledger cannot describe two runs — and a `model` input
plus a proposal step on `benchmark-agentic.yml`, gated on the key's presence through a materialised flag because the
`secrets` context is not readable from a step's `if`.

The engine's defaults are untouched. `absolute` is still the shipped gate mode, and the model arm changes no ranking
until a weight is passed and a claim is verified.

## 283. The operator was never the problem

§282 measured the model arm at 33.1 % against a 75.5 % control and named the failure as a **contract** defect: the
verifier wanted the cited channel on both candidates, the prompt asked for one on the removed candidate, and 33.2 %
of claims died there. The obvious repair was a better operator — the shipped arm *displaces* (a unary score
multiplier, so `weight = 1` erases rank 0), while a rank-fusion operator is pairwise and can express a tie.

This iteration implements the pairwise operators, implements the two nulls that say whether there is anything to
fuse, and reads both from the artifact §282 already paid for. **The operator is not the repair, and the contract was
not the whole defect.**

### The measurement that decides it

| quantity | reading |
| --- | --- |
| claims scored | 5 335 across 1 422 cases |
| **uniform null** (keep drawn from the same pool) | **519 hits (9.73 %) against 891 expected (16.70 %) — z = −14.41** |
| surviving `verifyClaim` | 3 321 of 5 335 (62.2 %) |
| uniform null, survivors only | 310 (9.33 %) against 529 expected — z = −11.00 |
| **constant swap** (promote rank 1 everywhere) | **1 073 → 112 of 1 422 (75.46 % → 7.88 %), delta −961** |
| claims promoting rank 1 | 4 113 (77.09 %) |
| claims exactly "remove rank 0, keep rank 1" | 1 318 |

`z = −14.41` is not a weak signal: it is a signal pointing the wrong way. The model's choice is **significantly
worse than a draw from the same pool**, and the mechanism is in the same table — 77.09 % of claims promote rank 1,
which is the truth in 112 of 1 422 cases. The arm's −602 is the constant rule applied to 925 cases; the corpus
scores the same rule applied to all 1 422 at −961.

| strategy | weight | correct | delta | moved | delta over survivors |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| control | 0 | 1 073 | — | 0 | — |
| `rrf` / `borda` | 0.2 | 1 073 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `rrf` / `borda` | 0.5 | 883 | −190 | 284 | −125 |
| `rrf` / `borda` | 1.0 | 882 | −191 | 287 | −155 |
| `veto` | 0.5 | 1 073 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `veto` | 1.0 | 147 | −926 | 1 381 | −600 |

**No positive region, at any weight, under any operator.** `rrf` and `borda` agree to the last digit because the
claims are almost all one claim; `veto` at full weight recovers the constant-swap null from the claim set alone. The
best an operator can do here is **0**, by moving nothing. And the shipped displacement arm is *better* than full
`veto` only because it moves fewer cases — a weakness that reads as an advantage.

### Three defects the tests found, all in the new module

- **Absence scored as "second".** `fuseRanks` ranked a service the second order omitted just after that order's last
  entry, so a second order naming one service out of five ranked the other four as second — a nearly empty opinion
  converted into a nearly full one. Absence now scores on the engine's order alone.
- **A removal outranked silence.** `impliedOrder` counted `keeps − removes`, and two services the model never
  mentioned outranked one it named as the thing to remove: "never mentioned" beat "mentioned as wrong". Counting
  promotions only is what a claim actually states.
- **An arm the comparator cannot reach.** A ternary in the tie-break had a branch that only fires when a ranked
  service is seated after an unranked one, which the row order makes impossible. Replaced by subtraction, because an
  arm nobody can reach is a branch nobody measures.

### What the literature says this failure is

arXiv:2608.21310 (October 2026) evaluates ten framework–backbone configurations on RCABench. **OpsAgent reads
45.8 %** with the note "issues no telemetry queries of its own, instead reasoning over a pre-extracted feature set"
— which is this project's model arm, catalogued before it was built. The best configuration reads **90.0 %**
(ThinkDepth.ai on Claude Sonnet 4.6), and every framework above 70 % runs
`while not committed: query = select_next_query(); result = telemetry.query(query)`. The paper's own intervention,
DiagGuard, adds **+9.0 pp** on a held-out model, dataset and topology with a Grounder (force systematic survey
before localising) and a Verifier (audit against evidence before committing), near-additively (+4.5 / +4.1).

Our artifact already shows the split the paper describes: the model is accurate where the task is **local and
checkable** (a cited channel is genuinely outside its band 98.6 % of the time) and at chance where the task is
**global** (pick the source among five). So the next arm asks for the local task and leaves ranking to the engine.

### Axes this closes

| Axis | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| "A better fusion operator recovers the arm" | **closed as REFUTED with numbers** — three operators × five weights × two populations, no positive delta; the proposal set is 14.4 σ on the wrong side of chance |
| "`weight = 0` means the model agrees" | **closed** — it is the engine's order returned unchanged before any arithmetic, for every strategy, so a delta at zero weight is a delta against the engine |
| "A veto can be dialled" | **closed** — a veto fires at `weight >= 1` or not at all; a half-veto has no definition and would be a scale nobody wrote down |
| "The failure is arithmetic" | **closed as refuted** — one `value-disagrees-with-fingerprint` in 5 335 claims; the failure is choice, not copying |
| "The failure is the channel contract" | **closed as insufficient** — repairing the contract admits 1 774 more claims whose truth rate is 9.6 %, so the repair changes nothing |
| "A model without query access is a competitive arm" | **closed by the literature and by our own reading** — the category is catalogued at 45.8 % on RCABench and ours reads 33.1 %; the ceiling for this shape is not a tuning gap |

### What ships

`docs/agentic-fusion.md` is the instrument record; this section is the verdict.
`packages/ai/src/agent/fusion.ts` (**100/100/100/100**, 29 tests — `rrf`, `borda`, `veto`, the implied order, and
the zero-weight control), `benchmarks/src/agentic-null-model.ts` (**100/100/100/100**, 12 tests — the uniform null
with its per-claim expectation and Bernoulli variance, and the constant-swap null), and two lines on the study's
output that print both nulls beside the arm they judge. The engine's defaults are untouched; no published number
moves, because the change is an instrument and a refusal.
